name: Commercial Intelligence for MedTech
blurb: AI tools that tell device sales teams where to focus.
title: Commercial Intelligence for MedTech
answer: Device makers use commercial intelligence platforms that combine procedure, claims and physician data to target sales effort, a market started by companies such as AcuityMD, which raised its seed round from Benchmark in 2021 and has since added agentic features.

reading.body:
Commercial intelligence for MedTech is a data-aggregation business before it is an AI business. The platforms combine procedure, claims and physician data to tell device sales teams which accounts to work, and the AI features sit on top of that assembled record.

The pattern is the same one that runs through most enterprise AI: the model is the cheap part, and the proprietary dataset is the product. AcuityMD raised a $7 million seed round led by Benchmark in May 2021 to close the medical device industry's information gap, and has since added agentic features. That sequence matters. The agentic layer arrived after the data position was established, not instead of it.

For AI specifically, this is a case where capability is bounded by data provenance rather than compute. Procedure data typically comes from insurance claims aggregated by data vendors, and physician-level detail carries rules: industry codes and laws govern interactions and payments to health care professionals. A sales team using these tools has to know where the data came from and what uses are permitted, because the targeting decision is only as defensible as its source.

What the data does not cover is scale. There is no market size, no adoption figure, no accuracy measure for the AI features, and no evidence on whether targeted outreach actually improves sales outcomes. It establishes that the category exists, who started it and when, and what the compliance surface looks like. It does not tell you how large it has become.

explainer:
Device companies sell to hospitals and surgeons, and their sales teams need to know who performs which procedures, where volumes are growing and which accounts use competitors' products. Commercial intelligence platforms combine claims, procedure and provider data to answer those questions and target effort.

AI features now summarise accounts, prioritise targets and draft outreach. The data often include detail at the level of individual physicians, so companies should understand its sources, how it was compiled and what uses are permitted, and keep outreach within industry codes on interactions with health care professionals.

What commercial intelligence means for device makers

Medical device companies sell through hospitals, surgeons, procurement groups and distributors rather than through prescriptions, so the signals that matter are different from pharma's. They include procedure volumes by hospital, capital budget cycles, tender timetables, competitor launches, recall notices, reimbursement code changes and which surgeons are publishing on a technique. Gathering these from public filings, tender portals, conference abstracts and regulator databases used to be a manual analyst job.

How AI changes it

Language models can read thousands of tender documents, filings and abstracts and extract the fields a commercial team cares about, then flag changes week to week. Combined with a company's own sales and service data, that gives territory teams a current picture of which accounts are likely to buy, replace or switch. The same tools summarise competitor regulatory filings and adverse event trends, which matter in device sales because a competitor's recall can open an account.

What to be careful about

Much of this information is public, but some of it is personal data about clinicians, and using it for targeting is regulated in several countries. Extracted fields can also be wrong, so anything that drives a sales action should link back to the source document. The strongest programmes keep humans deciding and use AI to make sure they decide with current information.
